t: Shortest Path in a Hidden Grid: Explore Then BFS
o: This interactive maze gives no dimensions, walls, or target upfront - only yes/no probes through GridMaster. The standard recipe: physically wander with a DFS while recording everything discovered into a coordinate map anchored at the start, then run BFS over the reconstructed open cells to get the minimum hop count. Example 1 walks up then right to discover the target two steps away; example 3 target sits in a region the robot never reaches, so exploration finds nothing and we return -1. Grids reach 500x500 = 250k cells, so an explicit stack beats recursion (which risks stack overflow) and each cell is probed at most four times.
k: Anchor an imaginary coordinate system at the start cell; every physical move mirrors a bookkeeping move, including the backtrack.
Record walls immediately whenever canMove fails - those neighbors must never be probed again.
Exploration (DFS) establishes connectivity and locates the target; BFS over the recorded open cells yields the shortest distance.

a.i: An explicit-stack DFS drives the robot through every open cell reachable from the start. Each probed neighbor is stored in a hash map keyed by coordinates with status open/target/wall. When the top cell has no unexplored neighbor, find the direction leading back to its parent, move once, and pop. Afterwards BFS from the start over recorded open cells returns dist(target); if the target was never mapped, it is unreachable.
s: Mark the start cell (checking isTarget) and push it onto the stack.
Loop: for the stack top, probe each direction whose neighbor is unmapped; on canMove success move, mark, push the child; on failure record a wall.
When no direction advances, move back to the parent and pop.
After exploration, BFS from (0,0) across mapped open cells counting hops.
Return the distance to the target, or -1 if it was never found.
a.t: O(m*n) - every cell is mapped once with at most four canMove probes, and BFS visits each mapped cell once
a.sp: O(m*n) - the coordinate map plus the stack and BFS queue

w: Interactive problems reward discipline: always undo a move during backtrack (step back toward the parent, not deeper), never re-probe a known wall, and simulate locally before submitting. Recursion risks stack overflow at 500x500 cells - the Python and JavaScript versions above use an explicit stack; convert the C++/Java versions similarly if limits are tight. Do NOT stop exploring early upon finding the target: a shorter route could leave the partially explored region, so finish mapping the connected component before BFS. Pitfalls: mispairing opposite directions (U/D and L/R) during backtracking, forgetting the initial isTarget check, and off-by-one coordinate keys. Follow-ups: weighted cells (Dijkstra on the discovered map), multiple targets, or minimizing query count.
